2. What the Brex Exit Means for Ramp (Not Ideal For Valuations, At Least)
Three things happened for Ramp investors on the same day:
The good news:
Brex essentially acknowledged Ramp won, even if they aren’t 100% direct competitors in every segment and with every product today. Started later, doing $1 billion to Brex’s $700 million.
The uncomfortable news:
When real money—not a secondary buyer purchasing 2% of the cap table—wrote an actual check for the whole asset, they valued it at 7x revenue. If you multiply Ramp’s billion-dollar run rate by 7, you get $7 billion. Even doubling it for faster growth gets you to $15 billion. Ramp raised at $32 billion.
The structural news:
Capital One now owns both Discover (closed for $50 billion) and Brex. Discover has a closed network—meaning Cap One captures all the interchange instead of splitting it with Visa and Mastercard. They can now route Brex spend onto their own rails.
If you’re Ramp, you’re now playing against the A-team with a structural cost advantage.
The mark-to-market conversation is going to be awkward: How do you factor in a comparable transaction at 7x revenue when your last round implied 30x?

Capital One just announced it’s acquiring Brex for $5.15 billion. An incredible, top 0.1% “exit” in less than 10 years from a category creator that created massive wealth and opportunities. A huge win. But also … less than half of Brex’s $12.3 billion valuation from October 2022. Should anyone care? Many are seeing is a failure vs Ramp, a measured success at best. But … why? I don’t think most people commenting on this actually understand what they’re reacting to. What they’re really feeling—even if they can’t articulate it—is the consequences of
hubristic fundraising
. And we should probably talk about it. Because hubristic fundraising is back. In a big way. It was back big time in 2025 and is back even bigger time in 2026. First, What Is Hubristic Fundraising? Let me define it simply: Hubristic fundraising is when you raise at a valuation so aggressive, with terms so favorable, with a narrative so bold, that you are essentially betting the entire future of your company on hitting an extraordinary outcome. It’s not just “raising a lot of money.” Plenty of companies raise hundreds of millions without hubris. Hubristic fundraising is when you:
Take a valuation that requires Top 0.1%+ annual growth for a decade to grow into
Raise at 100x-500x+ revenue multiple. Often, again and again. Build your entire talent acquisition, press strategy, and customer pitch around being “the most valuable” or “fastest-growing”
Create expectations that anything less than a $20B+ IPO or massive strategic exit is a disappointment
These deals can work out.

So I was asked recently what’s worse — when you hire an amazing VP of Sales that can’t really get going with your product … or one that does well for a while then just starts to fall off?
My take:
I think they are both tough, but probably the latter is tougher. Here’s why:
First, everyone knows a new VP of Sales has some time to figure things out after she joins. They know there will be a dip, even if they don’t expect it. And so you sort of hope the next month or two gets a little better, and then later you see improvement in the next quarter or two. So folks aren’t expecting perfection right away. At least most people aren’t.
Second, once a VP of Sales truly “gets” your product, they almost always start seeing some improvement. It doesn’t always show up on the dashboard (although sometimes it does), but it usually shows up somewhere. Maybe leads increase 15%, or conversion goes up 25%. Whatever it is, something improves.
And third, the company often rallies behind someone good. If your VP of Sales is doing OK, but isn’t getting anywhere near the level you’d hoped, you still rally behind them. You feel like they need another chance, or more resources, etc. And because you’re rallying behind her/him, it helps a bit.
What happens when you fire a VP of Sales who did OK for a while? Well, many times, nothing much changes. The existing reps keep selling, but at a lower rate than before. But then often, no one rallies behind anyone else. No one steps up. Everyone feels guilty they didn’t step up earlier. Guilt is hard to overcome. It’s harder than a simple dip. It’s hard to find a replacement that performs better than the prior VP of Sales. It’s hard to motivate the remaining folks under him/her.

. Because you’re going to need a team to sell. And recruiting great reps and making them successful is the #1 most important thing your VP Sales will do. And the great VP of Sales all know this. .

We found ourselves in the same situation when we built SaaStr.ai—we were getting slammed with inbound requests while struggling to keep up with basic business operations. Our team was drowning in manual tasks that required hours of time each week. What did we do? We used AI to automate those jobs. I did. And I was right — because personalization is where the magic happens in B2B software.
Think about it:
When your CRM knows exactly what deals your rep closed with John at Acme Inc. three years ago,
and
your sales automation system understands the exact objection patterns and buying stages that John’s team follows every time they evaluate new tools —
you’re not just sending generic emails.

Or a $100K deal into a $500K account with multiple stakeholders across the organization.
Or better yet, an upsell deal from $100K to $250K+ by showing value without even asking for more budget.

Take your top 10 customers who have expanded beyond initial contracts. Pull their entire interaction history — emails, meetings, support tickets, product usage patterns, event attendance records, any mention of competitors they might have made (because those signals are gold).
Then run it through a deep learning model trained specifically on identifying expansion opportunities based on past behavior.
What does that look like?

traces.answer: So who said that AI means everything in SaaS needs to be a personalized experience? Well, I think we all know this answer today, but if you go back and look at some of my earlier posts and talks, I didn't used to believe that way. Even though you probably cannot deliver that level of personalization today without AI. It still remains true because here's the thing: humans just aren't willing to do this kind of work anymore. There are so many jobs out there where humans just don't want to put in the effort. And that job has been handed off to agents, which is great. But what I'm saying is: let's really lean into that.
